Beautiful. What have you found to be your biggest challenge? Watching Alec Soth manhandle his 8x10 gets me tight in the pants and I fear I shoot too much film already that I'd end up bankrupt.

Two things I find most challenging:

  1. The process. I sometimes forget to close the shutter after composing, so when I pull the slide out the film is over exposed almost immediately. Or I forget to put on an ND filter after composing and wind up exposing the film several hundred times longer than it should be.

  2. Calculating long exposures. The reciprocity failure rate is highly variable depending on the scene you're exposing. I wind up with a lot of garbage shots that I thought would come out great and a lot of great shots that I wasn't very confident about.

I learned how to develop film specifically for shooting 4x5 because I was afraid of the cost. I'm conservative with what I shoot on sheet film because each sheet costs $1.28 if I'm using my regular B&W film (Ilford Delta 100). The developing chemicals are cheap enough over time to be negligible. I'm trying out color developing at home with (so far) mixed results, but I think I can improve on that. Over all, the cost hasn't been much of an issue, surprisingly.

Ah, gotcha so you're only shooting B&W. I home develop about 5 rolls of B&W (35 and 120) a week so no worries there and 4x5 that's not too bad for a sheet. hell, my instax cost almost as much and I shoot a shit ton of that.

Stop. you're supposed to say "it's horrible and expensive and it's not worth it", instead, I'm shopping again..

I've done one big batch of stuff with the C-41 kit from Tetenal with surprisingly ok results, so I do have a 10 pack of Portra 4x5 that I'm going to try out. But yes, I do mostly B&W. I can do 4 sheets at a time with the taco method in a regular Paterson tank, which isn't too bad. 4x5 isn't something I play around with, I try to make very shot count.

It's great and rather affordable and it makes me very happy :P

Look at the prices on KEH. I paid $150 for a lens that might be one of the sharpest lenses I've ever touched. You probably don't want a monorail body though, but that's just my opinion.
EVery now and then I look into 4x5. So far I just can't quite justify it. You ever take portraits with it? I am not a landscape person.

Nope, I'm the opposite. This was the first portrait I've done, and there is a long list of stuff I screwed up. I understand it's great for portraits though, because you can get insane subject isolation even with fairly wide lenses focused at a distance from the camera. Check the flickr Large Format group for some good examples.

Used equipment is pretty affordable these days. Check out KEH.com.

This is pretty much how I feel now as well. I still shoot other formats for various reasons, but as I've learned and used 4x5 gear it has become what I turn to shooting for my own enjoyment. Helps that I've rebuilt my kit to fit my travel and shooting needs compared to the kit I bought at the start.
Can you tell me about your kit? I've come up with a decent backpack arrangement but it's still rough with the tripod I have to bring along unless I'm on a bicycle.

Sure, I'd be glad to. I have one of the Calumet BP1500 bags, which with the dividers re-arranged has enough space to carry some 4x5 bodies or field cameras, 3-4 lenses on Linhof boards, about 6 film holders, meter, loupe, dark cloth, filters, and my tripod attached to the back.

My current kit consists of:

  • Toyo VX125
  • Nikkor SW 75mm f/4.5
  • Fujinon SW 105mm f/8
  • Fujinon CM-W 150mm f/5.6
  • Peak 7x loupe
  • Sekonic L-558R meter
  • Feisol CT-3442 tripod with a Feisol CB-50DC ball head

All of that along with accessories weighs around 15lbs, for me it has been manageable and I take it walking or hiking with me all over now. It's crazy, but that setup is actually lighter than my Rollei medium format setup, but mainly because the Rollei lenses are built like tanks.

What's the first song you can remember getting high to?

My friend had this cassette from a band none of us had ever heard of. Amazing artwork on the liner. He threw it in as we sparked up our first joint.

Sweet child o mine, guns and roses

I was sitting in my new dorm room (acted as a resort hotel during the summer tourist season). My new roommate asked if I had wanted to get high. Since I had managed to go all through high school having never been asked this question, I figured why the hell not.

We sat down at our table and he packed this greyish/black tube. He called it a steamroller. It looked neat. As he lit the bowl for me I filled the chamber. I looked at him quizzically and he said 'Move your hand and keep breathing in". After a massive coughing attack I was sitting there wondering if it was 'kicking in' and I could have sworn I could hear my heartbeat.

"Dude, I can hear my heartbeat" I say. "No, that's the music" he replies. I wait a few minutes and listen then finally hear the music start. "Oh, I like this, who is this?". "You've never heard Dark Side of The Moon? What the fuck are you?" My first stoner moment was realizing how much of a sheltered life I had really lived up to that point.

My first Pink Floyd experience was the morning after a high school party - if you can call five boys drinking a 6pack each a party.

We went outside and smoked up. Dylan's father knew what was up and mostly as a joke started up Shine On You Crazy Diamond.

Blew my mind. And probably led to one of my current favourite pastimes - getting stoned and listening to Pink Floyd while watching muted nature documentaries.

The first song I remember hearing after smoking when I was like 16 was Fallen Rock Zone, by Ra. It's a good enough song, but I only remember hearing it because I immediately changed it. I smoked on and off till I was like 24 then picked it up full time. The first time I purposefully listened to music while high, I listened to the Dark Side of the Moon on vinyl and it was everything I thought it'd be :)
